[[Eddie Robinson Award]] (1994) | CFBHOF_year = 2015 | CFBHOF_id = 2373}} }} '''James Patrick Tressel''' (born December 5, 1952) is an American politician and retired [[college football]] coach who has served as the 67th [[Lieutenant Governor of Ohio|lieutenant governor of Ohio]] since 2025. A member of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]], Tressel previously was the president of [[Youngstown State University]] from 2014 to 2023.{{Cite web |date=July 8, 2011 |title=Ohio State waives fine, instead will pay Tressel $52,250 |url=https://www.dispatch.com/story/sports/college/2011/07/08/ohio-state-waives-fine-instead/64580547007/#:~:text=Before%20his%20resignation%2C%20Tressel%20was,the%20end%20of%20June%2030th. |access-date=2025-06-14 |website=The Columbus Dispatch}} Before entering higher education administration and public office, Tressel was the head football coach of the [[Youngstown State Penguins football|Youngstown State Penguins]] and later the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]] from 1986 to 2010. His teams won five national championships (four with YSU during the 1990s, and one with OSU in 2002), earning him multiple Coach of the Year accolades and induction into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2015. Tressel was born in [[Painesville, Ohio]] and attended [[Baldwin Wallace University|Baldwin–Wallace College]], where he played football as [[quarterback]] under his father, [[Lee Tressel]]. He became Youngstown State's fourth head football coach in 1986 and remained there until 2000 before succeeding [[John Cooper (American football)|John Cooper]] as head coach at Ohio State in 2001. During his tenure as Ohio State's 22nd head football coach, Tressel's teams competed in three [[BCS National Championship Game]]s and his [[2002 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|2002 squad]] won a [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national title]], achieving the first 14–0 season record in major college football since the [[1897 Penn Quakers football team|1897 Penn Quakers]].{{cite news|url=http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m1208/is_48_225/ai_80680611 |title=Cougars deserve to celebrate – College Football/Insider – Brigham Young University football team |access-date=April 24, 2008 |work=The Sporting News |first=Tom |last=Dienhart |year=2001 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070223001620/http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m1208/is_48_225/ai_80680611 |issue=48 |volume=225 |archive-date=February 23, 2007 }} Tressel resigned from Ohio State in May 2011 amid an NCAA investigation into [[Ohio State University football scandal|improper benefits involving players]] during the 2010 season, which resulted in the university vacating victories from that year, including the [[2011 Sugar Bowl]]. He later served as a consultant for the [[Indianapolis Colts]] from 2011 to 2012 and as vice president of strategic engagement at the [[University of Akron]] from 2012 to 2014, before becoming president of Youngstown State University. On February 10, 2025, Governor [[Mike DeWine]] nominated Tressel as Ohio lieutenant governor;{{Cite web |last=Balmert |first=Jessie |date=February 10, 2025 |title=Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine picks former OSU Coach Jim Tressel to serve as lt. governor |url=https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/politics/2025/02/10/ohio-gov-mike-dewine-picks-jim-tressel-to-serve-as-lt-governor/77974547007/ |publisher=[[Columbus Dispatch]]}} he was confirmed on February 12 and sworn in on February 14.{{cite web |last=Smyth |first=Julie Carr |date=February 12, 2025 |title=Former Buckeyes football coach Jim Tressel confirmed as Ohio's lieutenant governor |url=https://apnews.com/article/buckeyes-coach-tressel-ohio-lieutenant-governor-vance-1de9a09fe038dc1d605b82ff5b93675d |access-date=February 12, 2025 |website=AP News}} ==Early life== Tressel was born on December 5, 1952, in [[Painesville, Ohio]], a suburb of Cleveland. He grew up in nearby [[Mentor, Ohio]], where his father, [[Lee Tressel]], was the football coach at [[Mentor High School]]. After a 34-game winning streak at Mentor, Lee coached at [[Massillon Washington High School]] for two seasons before being named the head football coach for [[Baldwin–Wallace College]] in [[Berea, Ohio]]. Tressel attended many of his father's games and practices, and developed a friendship with his neighbor and former [[Cleveland Browns]] player [[Lou Groza]]. Tressel's mother, Eloise Tressel, worked as the athletic historian at Baldwin–Wallace while his father was the head coach.{{cite web|url=http://www.dispatch.com/content/stories/sports/2009/02/25/osutressel.html|title=Tressel to speak at Statehood Day luncheon|publisher=Dispatch.com|access-date=September 6, 2011}} After graduating from [[Berea High School]] in 1971, Tressel played quarterback under his father at Baldwin–Wallace College. As quarterback, he earned four varsity letters and won all-conference honors as a senior in 1974. Tressel also joined the [[Alpha Tau Omega]] fraternity. In 1975, Tressel graduated from Baldwin–Wallace with a bachelor's degree in education.{{cite web|title=Tressel named Vice President of Strategic Engagement |url=http://www.uakron.edu/im/online-newsroom/news_details.dot?newsId=12aeee1b-5a28-495c-a9e7-2b2eebfcb39d&crumbTitle=Tressel%20named%20Vice%20President%20of%20Strategic%20Engagement|publisher=University of Akron|access-date=March 1, 2013|date=February 2, 2012}} ==Coaching career== ===Early positions=== After graduating from Baldwin–Wallace, Tressel became a graduate assistant at the [[University of Akron]]. He coached the quarterbacks, [[wide receiver|receivers]], and [[running back]]s, while earning a master's degree in education. In 1978, he left to become quarterbacks and receivers coach at [[Miami University]] in [[Oxford, Ohio]]. By 1981, he had left to become the quarterbacks coach at [[Syracuse University|Syracuse]]. In 1983, he was hired at Ohio State to be the quarterbacks and receivers coach. That year, OSU had a 9–3 record, including a 28–23 victory over [[University of Pittsburgh|Pittsburgh]] in the [[Fiesta Bowl]]; a 39-yard pass from quarterback [[Mike Tomczak]] to wide receiver [[Thad Jemison]] clinched the win with 39 seconds remaining in the game. In 1984, he was given the added responsibility of coaching the running backs. That year, the team became [[Big Ten Conference|Big Ten]] champs, played in the Rose Bowl, and [[Halfback (American football)|tailback]] [[Keith Byars]] finished second in the [[Heisman Trophy]] voting. In 1985, OSU defeated [[Brigham Young University|BYU]] in the Citrus Bowl.{{cite web|url=http://byucougars.com/files/media_guides/m-football/2010/tradition/bowl-1985.html|title=1985 Citrus Bowl|publisher=byucougars.com|access-date=February 2, 2012|archive-date=September 6, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906103704/http://byucougars.com/files/media_guides/m-football/2010/tradition/bowl-1985.html|url-status=dead}} ===Youngstown State=== At the end of the 1985 season, Jim Tressel left his position as assistant head coach at Ohio State to become head coach at Youngstown State University. In Tressel's first season as coach, Youngstown State finished with a 2–9 record. In his second season, Youngstown State finished the season with an 8–4 record and won the [[Ohio Valley Conference]] championship. From 1991 to 1994, Youngstown State played in the [[Division I-AA]] National Championship game four times. In 1991, Tressel won his first national championship, defeating [[Marshall University|Marshall]]; the victory made him and his father the only father-son duo to win national championships in college football at that time (Vince and Larry Kehres have also won national championships).{{Cite news|url=http://www.the-review.com/news/20171203/vince-and-larry-kehres-reach-400-wins-at-mount-union|title=Vince and Larry Kehres reach 400 wins at Mount Union|last=ZUPANIC|first=JEFFREY|work=The Review|access-date=December 11, 2017|language=en|archive-date=December 11, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171211105207/http://www.the-review.com/news/20171203/vince-and-larry-kehres-reach-400-wins-at-mount-union|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|url=http://voices.yahoo.com/jim-tressel-more-than-football-coach-98394.html |title=Jim Tressel: More Than a Football Coach |last=White |first=Mike |access-date=February 4, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140729002112/http://voices.yahoo.com/jim-tressel-more-than-football-coach-98394.html |archive-date=July 29, 2014}}{{unreliable source?|date=October 2015}} Youngstown State won two more national championships in the following three years: against Marshall in 1993 (who had defeated them in 1992) and [[Boise State Broncos football|Boise State]] in 1994. 1997 brought Tressel his fourth national championship with a 10–9 victory against [[McNeese State University|McNeese State]]. He earned his 100th win against [[Indiana State University|Indiana State]]. 1999 marked Tressel's ninth visit to the Division I-AA playoffs, but the team lost to a [[Paul Johnson (American football coach, born 1957)|Paul Johnson]] coached [[Georgia Southern University|Georgia Southern]] in the title game. 2000 presented Tressel with more success, leading Youngstown State to a 9–3 season and its 10th playoff appearance. During the 1990s, Youngstown State had a record of 103–27–2, the most wins by any Division I-AA team and fourth most of both Division I-A and I-AA combined.{{cite web |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/50435-some-of-the-best-college-football-programs-in-the-country-are-not-in-division-ia |title=Some of the Best College Football Programs in the Country Are Not in Division 1A |publisher=bleacherreport.com |last=Nethers |first=David |access-date=February 4, 2012}} Tressel's overall record at Youngstown was 135–57–2. He was also named Division I-AA Coach of the Year in '91, '93, '94, and '97.{{cite web |url=http://www.ohiostatebuckeyes.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/jim_tressel_57760.html |title=Jim Tressel Biography |access-date=June 26, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180627005153/http://www.ohiostatebuckeyes.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/jim_tressel_57760.html |archive-date=June 27, 2018 |url-status=dead }} In 1998, Tressel's reputation was blemished when it emerged that Ray Isaac, quarterback on his first national championship team, admitted to accepting massive benefits from [[Mickey Monus]], the founder of [[Phar-Mor]] and former chairman of the Youngstown State board of trustees. The NCAA had been tipped off about the violations in 1994, but dropped its inquiry after a cursory internal investigation by Youngstown State. The nature of the violations only came to light when Isaac admitted to tampering with a juror in Monus' first corporate fraud trial. It later emerged that Tressel had never met with Isaac during the initial 1994 investigation. Monus subsequently testified that when Isaac initially came to Youngstown State in 1988, Tressel called Monus and asked him to work out a job for Isaac. Youngstown State subsequently admitted to a lack of institutional control and docked itself scholarships. The NCAA ultimately faulted Tressel and Youngstown State for their cursory 1994 investigation, but did not cite them for wrongdoing.{{cite web |url=http://www.dispatch.com/content/stories/local/2011/07/16/tressel-had-early-history-of-warnings.html |title=Ohio State Football: Tressel had early history of warnings |access-date=February 2, 2012}} Youngstown State was also allowed to keep its 1991 title since the NCAA's statute of limitations had expired.Farrey, Tom. [https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=1920867 Souls of the departed haunt Youngstown]. [[ESPN]], November 12, 2004. On July 9, 2007, Jim and Ellen Tressel, along with Frank and Norma Watson, donated $1 million to Youngstown State University for the building of an indoor athletics facility named the Watson and Tressel Training Site. The facility opened for use in the fall of 2011."Youngstown State." Watson and Tressel Training Site. N.p., n.d. Web. December 12, 2013. This was the second major donation the Tressels and Watsons made to YSU. In 2003, they donated a combined $250,000 to the campaign for the Andrews Student Recreation and Wellness Center, which opened in 2005.{{cite web|url=http://www.ysu.edu/marketingComm/files/articles/1076/PDF/1076.pdf |title=Tressels, Watsons donate $1M to YSU campaign |access-date=November 25, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100602082621/http://www.ysu.edu/marketingComm/files/articles/1076/PDF/1076.pdf |archive-date=June 2, 2010}} ===Ohio State=== [[File:Coach Tressel.png|right|thumb|Tressel's [[sweater vest]] became a trademark for the coach, especially after he went to Ohio State.]] When [[John Cooper (American football)|John Cooper]] was dismissed as Ohio State's head football coach following a loss to unranked [[University of South Carolina|South Carolina]] in the [[2001 Outback Bowl]], Tressel returned to Ohio State as Cooper's successor. While addressing Buckeye fans during halftime of a basketball game just after being hired as head coach, Tressel declared, "I can assure you that you will be proud of your young people in the classroom, in the community, and most especially in 310 days [[Michigan–Ohio State football rivalry|in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on the football field]]."{{cite web|url=http://media.www.michigandaily.com/media/storage/paper851/news/2001/07/23/Sports/Tressel.Eyes.Finally.Bucking.The.Wolverines-1408404.shtml |title=Tressel eyes finally bucking the Wolverines |access-date=April 24, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071221173235/http://media.www.michigandaily.com/media/storage/paper851/news/2001/07/23/Sports/Tressel.Eyes.Finally.Bucking.The.Wolverines-1408404.shtml |archive-date=December 21, 2007}} Tressel coached the Buckeyes to two 19-game winning streaks, one which spanned the 2002 and 2003 seasons and the other which spanned the 2005 and 2006 seasons. Tressel's winning percentage at Ohio State of 81.0% (maintained over an extensive 10 seasons/116 games coached) is tied with [[John B. Eckstorm]] (29 games coached) for the second best in school history, behind only Carroll Widdoes' 16–2 (88.9%, 18 games coached) mark in the 1944–1945 seasons.{{cite web |url=http://ohiostatebuckeyes.com/fls/17300/pdf/fb/guide/08_Spring_p100to129.pdf?SPSID=87751&SPID=10408&DB_OEM_ID=17300 |title=Year-By-Year Coaching Records (page 108) |access-date=April 24, 2008 }}{{dead link|date=August 2017 |bot=Red Director |fix-attempted=yes }} Most importantly to many Buckeyes fans and former players, Tressel was 9–1 versus Michigan. As Ohio State's head coach, Tressel was known for a conservative style of play calling (dubbed "Tresselball"), winning games with just enough scoring, strong defense, and "playing field position."{{cite web |url=http://blog.cleveland.com/sports/2007/09/ohio_state_football_help_make.html |title=Ohio State football: Help make the pick |date=September 13, 2007 |access-date=April 24, 2008}} Tressel often referred to the punt as the most important play in football.{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/bowls06/columns/story?columnist=maisel_ivan&id=2722614 |title=Buckeyes buy Tressel's special teams message |date=January 7, 2007 |access-date=April 24, 2008}} He is sometimes referred to as "The Senator" (most notably by [[ESPN]]'s [[Chris Fowler]]), because of his composure on the sidelines during play and his diplomatic way of interacting with representatives from the media.{{cite web|url=http://cantonrep.com/printable.php?ID=403280 |title=Tressel wows crowd of Ohio lawmakers|access-date=April 24, 2008|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081201013300/http://cantonrep.com/printable.php?ID=403280 |archive-date=December 1, 2008 }} He is also referred to as "The Vest" for his penchant for wearing a [[sleeveless sweater|sweater vest]] on the sidelines.{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/bowls07/columns/story?id=3178400 |title=Tressel, Ohio State made for each other |date=January 3, 2008 |access-date=April 24, 2008}} Until his retirement, Tressel was one of only two active coaches with five or more national championships in any division{{cite web|url=http://onpointsportsblog.com/2011/05/breaking-news-jim-tressel-resigns/ |title=Breaking News: Jim Tressel resigns |publisher=onpointsportsblog.com |last=Napfel |first=Sean |access-date=February 4, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110609073203/http://onpointsportsblog.com/2011/05/breaking-news-jim-tressel-resigns/ |archive-date=June 9, 2011}} (only [[Larry Kehres]] of Division III [[Mount Union College]] has more with 10). He is the third Tressel to reach 100 wins, joining his father (155 wins) and his older brother, Dick (former OSU running backs coach), who coached at [[Hamline University]] (124 wins). As a family, with Jim's 229 wins, Lee, Jim, and Dick have won 508 games.Jim Tressel Biography During Tressel's first year (2001), Ohio State had a 7–5 record. Ohio State returned to the Outback Bowl, where the Buckeyes once again fell to South Carolina. Although the Buckeyes lost on a last-minute field goal, the team battled back to tie the game at 28–28 after being down 28–0.{{cite web |url=http://www.outbackbowl.com/facts/game02.html |title=Game Summary – January 1, 2002 |access-date=April 24, 2008}} Despite a second consecutive bowl loss and a 5-loss season, Tressel had coached the Buckeyes to a 26–20 upset victory over Michigan, fulfilling the promise he had made 10 months earlier. The following year (2002) Tressel and the Buckeyes became the first team in college football history to finish 14–0, defeating the heavily favored [[Miami Hurricanes|University of Miami]] Hurricanes in double overtime to win the [[2003 Fiesta Bowl]] and the 2002 National Championship. It was Ohio State's first national championship in 32 years. That success made him the first coach in NCAA history to win the AFCA's Coach of the Year award while at different schools; he is also the first to win the award in two different divisions.{{cite web |url=http://naia.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/011008aaa.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080517114941/http://naia.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/011008aaa.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 17, 2008 |title=Carroll's (Mont.) Mike Van Diest Wins 2007 AFCA Coach of the Year |access-date=April 24, 2008}} They were able to earn the national championship through close wins on a defensive-minded scheme that relied on field position. With a combination of senior leadership with [[Mike Doss|Michael Doss]] and freshman [[Maurice Clarett]], Tressel was able to pull out many close games during the season. Seven of their 14 victories were within 7 points including one overtime game against Illinois, and a double overtime game coming in the 2003 Fiesta Bowl.{{cite web |url=https://proxy.espn.com/college-football/columns/story?columnist=maisel_ivan&id=1662661 |title=Tresselball just keeps winning |date=November 15, 2003 |access-date=April 24, 2008}}{{cite web |url=http://www.ohiostatebuckeyes.com/SportSelect.dbml?SPSID=87745&SPID=10408&DB_OEM_ID=17300&KEY=&Q_SEASON=2002 |title=Football – 2002 Schedule & Results |access-date=April 24, 2008 }}{{dead link|date=April 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Coming off the national title season, the Buckeyes earned an 11–2 record in 2003, but the team lost to Michigan in the 100th meeting between the two teams 35–21. The Buckeyes finished the 2003 season with a 35–28 victory over Kansas State in the Fiesta Bowl on January 2, 2004. In 2004, the team finished 8–4, closing out the season with a 33–7 victory against [[Oklahoma State University - Stillwater|Oklahoma State]] at the [[Alamo Bowl]] and upsetting Michigan in the annual rivalry game. Ohio State was unranked and Michigan was ranked 7th and the final score was 37 to 21. During 2005, the Buckeyes had a 10–2 record which featured an early season loss to eventual BCS National Champion Texas and another in Happy Valley versus Penn State, who finished the season ranked third in the BCS. However, the season ended with the Buckeyes defeating [[University of Notre Dame|Notre Dame]] 34–20 in the [[Fiesta Bowl]]. The [[2006 Ohio State Buckeyes football team]] went undefeated in the regular season—including a 42–39 victory over Michigan which saw the first ever meeting between the two teams ranking numbers 1 and 2, respectively, in the national polls.{{cite web |url=http://www.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/stories/111106aem.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110622012453/http://www.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/stories/111106aem.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 22, 2011 |title=Finally, No. 1 Ohio State vs. No. 2 Michigan Is A Reality |access-date=April 24, 2008}} Ohio State finished second in the final [[2006 NCAA Division I-A football rankings|AP and Coaches polls]] after losing the [[2007 BCS National Championship Game]] to the [[2006 Florida Gators football team|University of Florida]], 41–14. In the 2007 season Jim Tressel led the 11–1 Buckeyes to a third consecutive Big Ten Championship and second consecutive National Championship berth, played January 7, 2008, against the [[LSU Tigers football|LSU Tigers]], in the [[Louisiana Superdome|Superdome]]. However OSU was beaten 38–24 by LSU, becoming only the second team to lose two consecutive BCS title games (the first being the University of Oklahoma).{{cite web |url=http://ohiostate.scout.com/2/717959.html |title=Buckeyes Again Fall Short In Title Game |access-date=April 24, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080820045500/http://ohiostate.scout.com/2/717959.html |archive-date=August 20, 2008 }} In 2008 Ohio State won their fourth straight Big Ten title. However, they lost the conference's automatic BCS berth and trip to the Rose Bowl on the head to head tiebreaker with a 13–6 loss to Penn State at home on October 26. The Buckeyes played Texas in the Fiesta Bowl, coming back from an 11-point second half deficit to take the lead with just over 2 minutes to play, only to lose when Texas scored with 16 seconds remaining. The 2009 team won its fifth straight conference title and earned a berth in the Rose Bowl against Oregon, winning the game 26–17. The 2010 OSU football season finished with the team posting a 12–1 record after beating Arkansas in the [[2011 Sugar Bowl]], 31-26. However, all of the wins were later vacated due to Tressel knowingly using ineligible players, leaving the team's "official" record for the campaign as 0–1. The Tressel family continued the tradition of supporting the campus where Jim coached. As co-chairs on the contribution campaign, Coach Tressel and wife Ellen made a sizeable donation toward the renovation of Ohio State's $109 million William Oxley Thompson Memorial Library. The fourth-floor outdoor Tressel Terrace honors them for their contribution. Tressel also promised continuing donations to the library through royalties from his book, "The Winners Manual."{{cite web |url=http://www.thelantern.com/campus/donors-vital-to-osu-library-revamp-1.527816#.TtBaJ3GXN38 |archive-date=September 12, 2012 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120912022639/http://www.thelantern.com/campus/donors-vital-to-osu-library-revamp-1.527816%23.TtBaJ3GXN38 |url-status=dead|title=Donors vital to OSU library revamp |access-date=November 25, 2011 }} The Tressel family also teamed with Ohio State's Comprehensive Cancer Center – James Cancer Hospital and Solove Research Institute by establishing, promoting and donating to the Tressel Family Fund for Cancer Prevention Research.{{cite web |url=http://cancer.osu.edu/waystogive/about/funds/tressel/Pages/index.aspx |title=The Tressel Family Fund for Cancer Prevention Research |access-date=November 25, 2011}} Both of Jim Tressel's parents died of cancer.{{cite web|url=http://www.sharingthevictory.com/vsItemDisplay.lsp?method=display&objectid=E4C94DB1-06DD-450D-BB7E2803FB55A6B3 |title=The Man in the Sweater Vest |access-date=November 25, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426002159/http://www.sharingthevictory.com/vsItemDisplay.lsp?method=display&objectid=E4C94DB1-06DD-450D-BB7E2803FB55A6B3 |archive-date=April 26, 2012 }} Further, the Tressels donated a monument titled "Traditions," erected in 2011 in a park near OSU's ROTC center. Remembrance park honors more than a thousand Ohio State alumni who, as military personnel, lost their lives in service to the United States.{{cite web|url=http://beta.wosu.org/news/2011/09/03/remembrance-park-at-osu-dedicated-tressels-attend/ |title=Remembrance Park At OSU Dedicated; Tressels Attend |access-date=November 25, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120404192305/http://beta.wosu.org/news/2011/09/03/remembrance-park-at-osu-dedicated-tressels-attend/ |archive-date=April 4, 2012 }} ====NCAA violations and resignation==== {{Main article|Ohio State University football scandal}} On March 8, 2011, Ohio State suspended Tressel for the first two games of the 2011 season and fined him $250,000 for failing to notify the school of NCAA violations involving Ohio State football players. The players had a financial arrangement with [[Edward Rife]], owner of a local tattoo parlor, who was at the time under investigation by the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]] for drug trafficking.{{cite web |last=May |first=Tim |url=http://www.dispatch.com/live/content/sports/stories/2011/03/10/source-of-e-mails-to-coach-revealed.html?sid=101 |title=OSU football: Source of e-mails to Tressel revealed | BuckeyeXtra |publisher=Dispatch.com |date=March 10, 2011 |access-date=May 31, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110516115417/http://www.dispatch.com/live/content/sports/stories/2011/03/10/source-of-e-mails-to-coach-revealed.html?sid=101 |archive-date=May 16, 2011 }} The arrangement, which resulted in five Ohio State football players being suspended, involved trading championship rings, jerseys, and other football-related awards for tattoos. That arrangement was a violation of NCAA rules, and would have rendered the players, including star quarterback [[Terrelle Pryor]], ineligible to play for portions of the 2010 season. Tressel was first notified of the arrangement in April 2010 when he received several e-mails from Chris Cicero, a local attorney and former Ohio State walk-on football player. Tressel never forwarded the e-mails, nor the information contained in them about potential violations, to his school's compliance office or the NCAA. Although Tressel had held the position of athletic director at Youngstown State, Tressel's excuse was that he did not know whom to contact when he learned of the alleged violations. Tressel also later claimed not to have acted because of concerns about the confidentiality of the information, yet he immediately forwarded the first e-mail to Terrelle Pryor's mentor. On December 7, 2010, Ohio State was notified by the Department of Justice that it had in its possession many items of Ohio State sports memorabilia seized from Edward Rife's tattoo parlor. In the ensuing investigation, Tressel was questioned by Ohio State on December 16 concerning his knowledge of the activities disclosed by the Justice Department (the sale of rings, jerseys, and football memorabilia to Rife). Tressel denied any specific knowledge of the violations, and claimed that he could not remember who had given him the vague information. A week later Tressel exchanged text messages with Cicero, the attorney who had originally notified him of the activities back in April. Tressel verified that the Justice Department matter involved the same players and issues as the April e-mails. Tressel remained silent, his long-time knowledge of the violations (and his subsequent intentional fielding of ineligible players throughout the season) revealed only when Ohio State inadvertently discovered the April 2010 Cicero e-mails in an unrelated search in January 2011.{{cite magazine|last=Staples|first=Andy|title=Tressel gets two-game suspension, $250K fine for rules violation|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2011/football/ncaa/03/08/ohio-state-tressel-violation/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110310160720/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2011/football/ncaa/03/08/ohio-state-tressel-violation/|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 10, 2011|magazine=Sports Illustrated|access-date=March 8, 2011|date=March 8, 2011}}{{cite web|title=Ohio State football: Tressel's emails were forwarded|url=http://www.dispatch.com/live/content/sports/stories/2011/03/25/tressels-emails-were-forwarded.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120728102328/http://www.dispatch.com/live/content/sports/stories/2011/03/25/tressels-emails-were-forwarded.html|archive-date=July 28, 2012}}url=http://www.osu.edu/news/ncaadocs/ On March 17, 2011, it was announced that Tressel requested Ohio State Athletic Director [[Gene Smith (athletic director)|Gene Smith]] that he extend his own suspension to the same number of games as his players. Smith accepted the request, meaning Tressel would have sat out the first five games of the 2011 season.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/03/18/sports/ncaafootball/18tressel.html|title=Tressel Requests Five-Game Suspension|last=Thamel|first=Pete |author-link=Pete Thamel |date=March 17, 2011|work=The New York Times|access-date=March 18, 2011}} {{quote box|align=right|width=33%|quote = No, are you kidding? ... I'm just hoping the coach doesn't dismiss me.|author=Ohio State President Gordon Gee, when asked whether he would fire Tressel{{cite news|url=http://www.thelantern.com/sports/give-tressel-the-boot-1.2083500?firstComment=100 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130204034410/http://www.thelantern.com/sports/give-tressel-the-boot-1.2083500?firstComment=100 |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 4, 2013 |title=Give Tressel the boot |work=The Lantern |access-date=May 30, 2011 |author=Freking, Grant |location=Columbus, Ohio }}}} Ohio State President [[E. Gordon Gee|Gordon Gee]] assured the public that Tressel would not lose his job over the matter.{{cite web|title=Ohio St suspends Tressel 2 games for violation|url=http://www.ajc.com/sports/ohio-st-suspends-tressel-865154.html|publisher=e Atlanta Journal-Constitution|access-date=March 8, 2011}} On April 25, 2011, the NCAA accused Tressel of withholding information and lying to keep Buckeyes players on the field. In a "notice of allegations" sent to Ohio State, the NCAA charged that Tressel's actions were considered "potential major violations" which had "permitted football student-athletes to participate in intercollegiate athletics while ineligible." The report also said he "failed to comport himself ... (with) honesty and integrity" and that he lied when he filled out a compliance form in September stating that he had no knowledge of NCAA violations by any of his players.{{cite news |last=Miller |first=Rusty |title=NCAA alleges Tressel lied to hide NCAA violations |url=http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/stories/F/FBC_OHIO_ST_TRESSEL?SITE=AP&SECTION=HOME&TEMPLATE=DEFAULT |access-date=April 26, 2011 |agency=Associated Press |date=April 25, 2011 |archive-date=December 1, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241201000611/http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/stories/F/FBC_OHIO_ST_TRESSEL?SITE=AP&SECTION=HOME&TEMPLATE=DEFAULT |url-status=dead }} Tressel later stated that he lied about the violations because he didn't want to jeopardize the FBI's investigation against Rife and also feared for his players' safety. Despite his stated safety concerns, Tressel only briefly spoke with two players, never inquired of the two if other players were involved and also in danger, nor in his discussions with players ever mentioned Mr. Rife, the tattoo parlor, or the selling of Ohio State merchandise.[[Mark Schlabach|Schlabach, Mark]]. [https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/7373708/ncaa-sends-message-sanctions-ohio-state-buckeyes NCAA sends message to Ohio State]. [[ESPN]], December 20, 2011. The NCAA's report explicitly refuted the credibility of this excuse. Tressel resigned as Ohio State's head football coach on May 30, 2011.{{cite news|last=Rittenburg|first=Adam|title=Report: Jim Tressel tenders resignation|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=6606999&campaign=rss&source=ESPN|date=May 30, 2011}} Three days earlier, ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' reported that it had found evidence that the memorabilia-for-tattoos scandal dated back to at least the 2002 national championship season, and as many as 28 players were involved. Early on the morning of Memorial Day, Gee and Smith called Tressel back from his vacation in Colorado and asked for his resignation.{{cite magazine|author=George Dohrmann|author2=David Epstein|title=SI investigation reveals eight-year pattern of violations under Tressel|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2011/magazine/05/30/jim.tressel/index.html|magazine=Sports Illustrated|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110601073004/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2011/magazine/05/30/jim.tressel/index.html|url-status=dead|date=May 30, 2011|archive-date=June 1, 2011}}Dohrmann, George, "The Fall of Jim Tressel", ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'', June 6, 2011, pp. 40–48. ''[[The Columbus Dispatch]]'' reported that Gee had appointed a special committee to examine the scandal's impact on the school. It also reported that Ohio State had been looking to cut ties with Tressel for several weeks.{{cite news|author=Mike Wagner|author2=Ken Gordon|author3=Jiil Riepenhoff|title=Sources: Ohio State Coach Jim Tressel was encouraged to resign|publisher=[[The Columbus Dispatch]]|date=May 30, 2011}} Tressel said in a statement released by the university, "After meeting with university officials, we agreed that it is in the best interest of Ohio State that I resign as head football coach. The appreciation that Ellen and I have for the Buckeye Nation is immeasurable." [[Luke Fickell]], previously co-defensive coordinator and assistant head coach, was head coach for the 2011 football season.{{cite web|title=Tressel resigns at Ohio State|url=http://msn.foxsports.com/collegefootball/story/Jim-Tressel-resigns-as-Ohio-States-football-coach-053011|work=Fox Sports|access-date=May 30, 2011}} Tressel left Ohio State as the third-winningest coach in school history, behind Woody Hayes and John Cooper. However, on July 8, 2011, Ohio State vacated all of its wins from the 2010 season and placed the football program on two years' probation.{{cite news|title=Ohio State vacates 2010 wins, puts self on probation|url=http://news.blogs.cnn.com/2011/07/08/ohio-state-vacates-2010-wins-puts-self-on-probation/|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120711040658/http://news.blogs.cnn.com/2011/07/08/ohio-state-vacates-2010-wins-puts-self-on-probation/|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 11, 2012|publisher=CNN|access-date=July 8, 2011|date=July 8, 2011}} On December 20, 2011, the NCAA placed Ohio State on an additional one year's probation and banned it from postseason play in 2012 for numerous major violations under Tressel's watch. It also imposed a five-year [[show-cause penalty]] on Tressel, which means any NCAA member that wants to hire him would have to "show cause" for why it shouldn't be sanctioned for hiring him, and could face severe penalties if he commits any further violations during that time. The order stood until December 19, 2016; given past precedent, this likely had the effect of blackballing Tressel from the coaching ranks until the 2017 season. Had Tressel coached during this period, he would have been suspended for the first five games of the regular season, plus any conference championship game or bowl game. ===Indianapolis Colts=== On September 2, 2011, Tressel was hired by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] as a game-day/replay consultant. Tressel was suspended by the Colts until the 7th game of the season due to his involvement in the NCAA violations during his tenure as head coach at Ohio State. ==Administrative career== On February 2, 2012, Tressel accepted a non-athletic-department position where he started his coaching career, the [[University of Akron]].{{cite web|title=Tressel named Vice President of Strategic Engagement|url=http://www.uakron.edu/im/online-newsroom/news_details.dot?newsId=12aeee1b-5a28-495c-a9e7-2b2eebfcb39d&pageTitle=UA%20News&crumbTitle=Tressel+named+Vice+President+of+Strategic+Engagement|publisher=The University of Akron}} His title was Vice President of Strategic Engagement. In January 2013, various media reports stated that Tressel would possibly return to Youngstown State University to replace retiring [[Chancellor (education)|university president]] Cynthia Anderson as the next president of the university. Tressel was still revered in the area and a new athletic training complex bearing his name, the Watson and Tressel Training Site, opened on campus in 2011.{{Cite web|url=http://www.ysusports.com/information/facilities/watts|title=YSU Athletics Facilities - Youngstown State University}} However, Tressel's highest level of education is a master's degree; a doctorate is commonplace for a university president position in the United States. Combined with the [[show-cause penalty]] that was in effect for Tressel until 2016, on paper it would have been a tough sell for YSU to bring back Tressel. Supporters for bringing back Tressel also cited this, but mentioned that as university president, his primary job would be for [[fundraising]], in which Tressel had previously excelled over the years as head coach at both YSU and Ohio State.http://www.wkbn.com/content/news/local/story/Search-for-New-YSU-President-Begins/GhL5IUAKt0GAbbyXyGqPrw.cspx{{dead link|date=August 2017 |bot=Red Director |fix-attempted=yes }}{{cite web|url=http://www.vindy.com/news/2013/jan/13/ysu-president-tressel/|title=YSU President Tressel?|website=Vindy.com|access-date=March 24, 2013|archive-date=May 12, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130512041113/http://www.vindy.com/news/2013/jan/13/ysu-president-tressel/|url-status=dead}} On May 10, 2013, [[Randy Dunn]] was chosen as successor to Anderson,{{cite web|url=http://www.vindy.com/news/2013/may/11/dunn-deal-ysu-selects-new-president/|title=YSU's next president to start July 15|website=Vindy.com|access-date=May 15, 2013|archive-date=October 4, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004232041/http://www.vindy.com/news/2013/may/11/dunn-deal-ysu-selects-new-president/|url-status=dead}} but only stayed on the job for seven months, ultimately leaving for [[Southern Illinois University]]. After Dunn's sudden departure, Tressel's name again came up as a possible replacement. Tressel officially applied for the position on April 13, 2014; at the same time he remained one of 19 candidates for the University of Akron president's job.{{cite web | last=Hinnen | first=Jerry | title=Jim Tressel applies to become Youngstown State president | website=CBS Sports | date=2014-04-13 | url=https://www.cbssports.com/college-football/news/jim-tressel-applies-to-become-youngstown-state-president/ | access-date=2026-03-10}} Nearly a month later, on May 9, 2014, the YSU Board of Trustees, by unanimous vote, offered Tressel the position of university president.{{cite web |date=May 9, 2014 |title=Youngstown State offers president's job to Jim Tressel |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/college/2014/05/09/jim-tressel-president-youngstown-state/8890369/ |access-date=May 31, 2026 |website=[[USA Today]]|agency=[[Associated Press]]}} Tressel accepted, and announced that he was officially retired from coaching.{{Cite web |date=2014-05-09 |title=Youngstown St. offers presidency to Tressel |url=https://www.espn.com/college-sports/story/_/id/10906679/jim-tressel-offered-president-job-youngstown-state |access-date=2024-12-04 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press |language=en}} He held the university president job for nearly a decade. On June 23, 2022, Tressel announced his retirement from the position, effective February 1, 2023.{{cite web | last=DeNatale | first=Dave "Dino" | title=Jim Tressel to depart as Youngstown State University president in February 2023 | website=wkyc.com | date=2023-02-01 | url=https://www.wkyc.com/article/news/local/ohio/jim-tressel-departing-youngstown-state-university-president-february-2023/95-33074801-f2fa-45e0-88ea-e4e294df3528 | access-date=2024-12-04}} As Youngstown State president, Tressel was credited for increasing graduation rates from 35 to 49%, quadrupling the size of the Honors College, and adding hundreds of units of dormitories and apartments to increase the number of students living on or near campus. Tressel helped lead a delegation to obtain $10 million in federal funds to improve roadways around the university. He also fostered closer ties with the business community, creating an Excellence Training Center which offers certificates to students for in demand jobs, and aligning research with the needs of local businesses. The university raised over $150 million during Tressel's tenure.{{Cite web |date=February 2, 2023 |title=Looking at 'The Tressel Years': A lasting impression |url=https://www.wkbn.com/news/local-news/looking-at-the-tressel-years-a-lasting-impression/ |access-date=May 13, 2023 |website=WKBN.com |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Nelson |first=George |date=January 25, 2023 |title=Tressel Reflects on Time as YSU President |url=https://businessjournaldaily.com/tressel-reflects-on-time-as-ysu-president/ |access-date=May 13, 2023 |website=Business Journal Daily {{!}} The Youngstown Publishing Company |language=en-US}} ==Lieutenant Governor of Ohio (2025–present)== On February 10, 2025, Ohio Governor [[Mike DeWine]] nominated Tressel to serve as Ohio's 67th lieutenant governor after [[Jon Husted]] was appointed by DeWine to fill the Senate seat vacated by [[JD Vance]], who resigned after being elected [[Vice President of the United States]].{{Cite web |title=Governor DeWine Nominates Jim Tressel for Lt. Governor |url=https://governor.ohio.gov/media/news-and-media/governor-dewine-nominates-jim-tressel-for-lt-governor |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250211031134/https://governor.ohio.gov/media/news-and-media/governor-dewine-nominates-jim-tressel-for-lt-governor |archive-date=February 11, 2025 |access-date=2025-02-14 |website=governor.ohio.gov |language=en }} The [[Ohio General Assembly]] subsequently confirmed Governor DeWine's nomination, and Tressel was officially sworn into office in the Rotunda of the [[Ohio Statehouse]] on February 14.{{Cite web |date=2025-02-14 |title=Jim Tressel Sworn In as Ohio's 67th Lieutenant Governor |url=https://governor.ohio.gov/media/news-and-media/jim-tressel-sworn-in-as-ohios-67-lieutenant-governor |access-date= 2025-02-14 |website=governor.ohio.gov}}  Tressel confirmed that he was considering a [[2026 Ohio gubernatorial election|2026 run for governor]] on May 8, 2025, but later declined to run.{{Cite web |last=Gomez |first=Henry J. |date=2025-05-08 |title=Ohio Lt. Gov. Jim Tressel confirms he's considering a run for governor |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/elections/ohio-lt-gov-jim-tressel-confirms-considering-run-governor-rcna205734 |access-date=2025-06-07 |website=NBC News}}{{Cite web |last1=BeMiller |first1=Haley |last2=Balmert |first2=Jessie |date=2025-09-19 |title=Ohio Lt. Gov. Jim Tressel won't run for governor in 2026, clearing GOP field for Ramaswamy |url=https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/politics/2025/09/19/jim-tressel-wont-run-for-ohio-governor-in-2026/86242220007/ |access-date=2025-09-19 |website=The Columbus Dispatch |language=en-US}} He announced the statewide "Team Tressel Fitness Challenge" on August 25, designed to encourage elementary and middle schoolers to develop fitness and sleep routines.{{Cite web |date=2025-08-25 |title=Lt. Gov. Tressel announces launch of fitness challenge in Ohio schools |url=https://www.10tv.com/article/news/local/team-tressel-fitness-challenge-in-ohio-schools/530-5b516754-5fd2-4c48-8ce0-958023b0ff02 |access-date=2025-08-27 |website=10tv.com |language=en-US}} ==Personal life== Tressel and his wife Ellen, a [[Youngstown State]] graduate, are actively involved with the Fellowship of Christian Athletes, Athletes in Action, the OSU Thompson Libraries and The Ohio State University Medical Center, particularly the James Cancer Center. Tressel has three children from a prior marriage: Zak, Carlee, and Whitney; Ellen has one, Eric. He currently lives in the [[Youngstown, Ohio|Youngstown]] area.{{cite web|url=http://www.thewinnersmanual.com/bio.asp |title=About Coach Tressell |publisher=thewinnersmanual.com |access-date=February 4, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111024235445/http://www.thewinnersmanual.com/bio.asp |archive-date=October 24, 2011 }} Jim's brother, [[Dick Tressel]], was his running backs coach at Ohio State for seven seasons after serving as the head coach at [[Hamline Pipers football|Hamline University]] for 23 seasons. Dick's son, and Jim's nephew, is [[Mike Tressel]], the defensive coordinator at the University of Wisconsin.{{Cite web |title=Mike Tressel {{!}} Football Coach
